newsitem.title: HONG KONG: We're not misers -- HK's Financial Secretary.
newsitem.headline: We're not misers -- HK's Financial Secretary.

text.p: Hong Kong's top financial official hit out at critics on Friday who accused the government of drafting a miserly budget at a time when the British colony is expecting another fabulous windfall surplus.

Financial Secretary Donald Tsang, who is due to deliver his 1997/98 budget speech next Friday, said Hong Kong had been generous in increasing welfare spending while sticking firmly to its strict and prudent guidelines of not spending more than it earns.
"Over the last five years, we have increased social welfare spending by 86 percent in real terms," Tsang told reporters.
He said that this fiscal year alone, Hong Kong's social spending had increased more than nine percent in real terms.
Hong Kong, a wealthy community of 6.4 million people, enjoys one of the more extensive welfare systems in Asia, but it is rudimentary when compared with Western Europe.
The government has said it planned to spend more than HK$202.23 billion ($26 billion) in fiscal 1997, which starts in April.
But critics have said they expect Hong Kong to enjoy a windfall surplus of up to HK$25 billion for 1996/97, and argue that Tsang should be more generous.
Tsang is expected to unveil a conservative budget for the coming year -- which spans the handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1.
The Hong Kong government has denied that China was responsible for applying the spending brakes.
China accused the outgoing colonial government of introducing rampant welfarism into laissez-faire Hong Kong in the final years of British rule. ($1 = $HK 7.8)
